overview: Concierges help hotel guests, residents and members get what they need. They make dinner and spa reservations, arrange transport and tours, give directions and recommend local shopping and entertainment. O*NET rates knowledge of customer service at 4.73 out of 5 for this job, and active listening and speaking at 4. No degree is required: 46% have a high school diploma and 27% some college in O*NET data. The BLS May 2025 median is $38,950 across 49,240 jobs. Hours often include evenings and weekends, but the job offers variety and constant contact with people.
pay: Concierges earn a median of $38,950, and the top 10% earn $57,570 or more, before tips. Hawaii has the highest state median at $60,090, 54% above the national figure. New York has the most concierges, 6,040, at a median of $57,570, while Florida has 5,380 at $35,660.

faq.a: The BLS May 2025 median is $38,950 a year. The middle half earn between $35,660 and $47,350, and tips at luxury hotels can add a lot. Hawaii, New York ($57,570) and Rhode Island ($54,850) pay the most, while Alabama and Oklahoma pay the least.

faq.q: Do you need a degree to be a concierge?
faq.a: No. In O*NET data, 46% of concierges have a high school diploma, 27% some college courses and 9% a bachelor's degree. O*NET places the job in Job Zone 2. Hotel experience, local knowledge and a second language help most when applying to luxury properties.

O*NET rates active listening and speaking at 4 out of 5 for this job. Knowledge of customer service is rated 4.73, and empathy and social orientation stand out as work styles. Good concierges also build contacts with restaurants, drivers and venues.

The closest moves are reservation and ticket agents (91% match), hotel desk clerks (88%) and Travel Agents (81%), based on O*NET 31.0. Travel Agents earn $50,160, 29% more than concierges, according to BLS May 2025 data, and use the same planning skills.
